Master Xishi Chanshi, Dān-gōng, was like a resounding golden nail, his brilliance shining brightly amidst the monastic groves. All said that he was one capable of supporting and expanding our school.

Great officials and eminent scholars all arose with reverence and faith; the assembly of monks bowed in submission. His transformative influence spread daily toward the east. He was cremated.
If even those who obtain a mere fragment of his relics know to cherish them as treasures, then those who have been struck by the light of his teachings and aspire to behold him must surely be many.

Even a stubborn person must sneeze.

A single fragment. One does not know where its boundaries lie.

The descendants of Linji do not accept being examined or awakened; their eight facets are naturally rounded and clear, their steep precipice so formidable that who would dare to peer?

The bells chime *ding-dong* as at the beginning of the kalpa, yet for long there has been no man of true character to dwell here. How sad for the patrons! May you be spared such grief.

The original text: *Yuandu*. When the time of *Pou* (the hexagram of obstruction) reaches its limit, *Tai* (the hexagram of prosperity) arrives. He selects the "Iron-Faced Stubborn Old Man" to reside there. Carrying upside-down a handleless broom, he sweeps away the fox tracks accumulated over generations.

Turning over the eel-well, he leads others to the Cao Yuan (the source of Caoxi). Vast and surging, it flows and overflows through rivers and lakes with nowhere to rest. Is this not superior to the Yue song: "Why has it come so late? Throughout his life, he has been without... Translation: Yuandu. When the time of obstruction (*pou*) reaches its ultimate point, prosperity (*tai*) arrives. He appoints the "Iron-Faced Stubborn Old Man" to dwell there. Carrying inverted a handleless broom, he completely sweeps away the fox tracks accumulated over generations.

By overturning the eel-well, he leads others to the Cao Source. Vast and surging, it flows and overflows through rivers and lakes, finding no place to rest. Is this not far superior to the Yue song: "Why has it come so late? Throughout his life, he has been without [attachment].
The short tunic now has five layers of trousers.
Listening to the *wú* and *jiǎn* horns, I am moved; I bid farewell to the monk Yǎn as he returns to his hometown.
Upon the back of the Yellow Ox, the *wú* and *jiǎn* horns sound, blowing note after note as the music of the village fields. They sink low into the deep abyss and soar high—
Yun: To attempt to distinguish the *gong* and *shang* notes is entirely an error. Smoke is cut off as it flickers out to the west of Zhagang Hill;
this "wu-yi" calls out to that "ming-yi. Heaven and earth open wide and vast, and all movement ceases. Wildflowers bloom in surprise upon branches that never sprouted.
Throughout antiquity and today, how many have sung in response? One remembers the whole, yet forgets half. The wooden man skillfully plays the stringless lute; the stone woman...
Presented upon felt and cypress-wood boards: In years past, the rhythmic cadence was always surpassed by you; having heard it through until there is no sound, one returns to hearing itself.
When the song of returning home is played, people listen mistakenly, gathering their heads to call it the "Plum Blossom Melody."
Shun’s attendant dwells in his own clumsiness. He requests words to awaken those across the great earth who seek cleverness;
you alone preserve your clumsiness—eating your rice while holding the spoon upside down, and turning your socks inside out as they prick your eyes.
One knows only to sit idly by the stump; one does not worry about soaring eloquence like the moon. The true nature of heaven remains undivided—a single mass of chaotic iron.
Clutching the uncut jade, one seeks a forge and hammer, yet even a skillful hand finds it difficult to apply them. Come now, I resort to the clumsy beauty of the shadows;
with felt clappers, I join the stringless lute. Plucking yellow willow blossoms, I laugh heartily; even the woodsmen and cowherds are all connoisseurs of this sound. Is it not so?

As for those who see the path of the ridge: they have broken seven meditation cushions until not a single seam remains; they have turned their bodies within the ghost-cave and cried out that it was a great relief.
When the curtain is rolled up, the whole world is seen. Yet one does not see Master Long; this is the sleeping tiger of our house.

His spirit is stern as the autumn wind, his fangs and claws exposed; he sweeps the traces from a thousand forests, leaving no foxes or hares behind. One must know that skillfulness emerges from clumsiness. Skillfulness...
At the end of my clumsiness, there is nowhere to be found; where there is no seeking, one knows the essential point. Hurry, and I shall give you a blow from my rough fist.
Zen practitioner Kō from Japan: returning to your home country, you seek words;
from the land of Great Tang to the land of Japan, you let loose a falcon from the vast heavens before the wind. Without being separated by the deep ocean, you have seen it intimately.
Yet one remains separated by the vast deep ocean. Master Guang, reckless and heedless of his very life, bit down on his teeth and sought with all his might.
Amidst a mass of white waves, he launched a single reed raft. Though the *Putong* era is distant, it is just like today. Burning incense, you strike upon the meaning of my coming from the West.
With thirty blows of the black staff, I have struck out the very marrow. It is not Buddha, not things, and not mind either. To hesitate is like white clouds.
Ten thousand miles away, they have formed a grievance so deep that heaven cannot bear it. With a rage that steams like clouds, he strides out the door;
this time he must seek a clear resolution. He returns to question his father, Elder Master Long.
The Japanese Zen practitioner Jiyuan has returned to his country and requested a verse from me.
This year he is sixty-eight years old; he has closed himself in seclusion by a lake to cultivate his simplicity. Ten thousand conditions do not hang upon a single strand of hair;

when facing guests, he is too weary to employ his three-inch tongue. When asked about the Way, he says: "The rice paddies are drenched in green; the farmers boast of their excellence. When asked about me, he says: [He points to the text].
Zen. In the misty forests, the evening sounds have not yet been heard; for no reason, the foreigner has deceived me. Plugging in a piece of wood—what is one seeking?
Having drunk a cup of coarse tea, he is sent out the gate. On the sea mountains, the birds crying "return home" cease their lamentation.
At the request of the Japanese Zen practitioner Gen-shi, the Master spoke these words:

"From childhood you bore the ambition to soar above the clouds. Now at twenty-two, having become a monk at fifteen, you do not fear the treacherous waves of the great ocean as though they were precipitous cliffs.

You have traveled afar to clarify the intent of the Western Patriarchs. Beneath the shade of ancient pines, you knock upon the smoke-filled door; yet you have not yet penetrated the 'Splitting of Ci-xi'."
A mechanical arrow; his mouth full of local dialect, yet he studies the language of Tang. The people of the capital call him "Nasiqi.
With a coarse fist, he is about to strike across the chest. Yet, fearing that onlookers might judge whether he missed or hit, he hastens back to inquire of the old master who transmits the robe.
Cease staring at the cold spring water of the ancient ravine.
A View of Japan for Zen Practitioner Yong:
The Japanese realm and the Great Tang realm share a single imperial wind without any interval between them, like placing a jujube leaf upon the point of a needle.
When the heel of a straw sandal is torn away, heaven and earth seem narrow. You, Master, carry a mass of doubt within your breast; distinguishing between the barbarians and the Chinese, you strike—

In the intervals between herding, I am old and weary, unable to explain it in detail. Amidst the forest, spring birds warble with lingering, melodic cries. I shall now clearly raise this for you at the critical moment:
do not involve yourself in the subtleties of transcendence or immanence, but quickly take it up! The mysterious barrier of the Buddhas and Patriarchs has been overturned;
the golden sun flies upon the coral tree.

Showing the path of the Jewel Dhūta at Mount Jing, the striking of the bell divides the dreams and slumbers of weary lives. Deeply reflecting, from where does this single sound arise? A traveler’s boat is moored in the maple grove at midnight;
a monk knocks at the misty temple under the evening moon. How can these compare to the summit of Mount Lingxiao, where the roar of the wrathful whale resounds through the thousands?
The autumn forest: those who eat their fill and sleep do not understand this. Having eyes yet being as if blind, will you still listen? I have realized the nature that is beyond hearing;
though I speak it to the *dhūta*, he will never believe. If he does not believe, try returning and striking [the bell] and see:
the wind carries falling petals, and the mountain air is cold.

In the mountain hut where yams are roasted, one knows not the face of the spring breeze. Red and soft, the yams are cooked by the embers of the hearth fire. Cold tears hang from the chin as the midday dream awakens;
the hungry bowels rumble like rolling thunder in the clear sky. Frosty monkeys gnaw at the bark and open the cave door, leaking forth the celestial fragrance.
Emerald peaks, veiled by mists and smoke that cannot be gathered; they casually beckon the white clouds home.
Upon a broken wisteria bed, one’s livelihood is complete. With earth and ash, one splits soft jade. Letting go of folly, once sated, all conditions are empty.

Singing with the mountains, one strokes the belly with the hand. With whom can this true flavor be discussed? To roast the麒麟 (qílín) and mince the 鳳凰 (fènghuáng) is but a source of stench and grease. Had it been otherwise...
Lan Can knew of this; how could he deign to dazzle the Son of Heaven with empty fame?
A young servant boy gathered shepherd’s purse, carrying his basket away; he searched through crumbling walls and desolate gardens until the roots turned a faint yellow at dawn.

Frost. Leaves spread a tender green, nourished by the spring rain. A sand-pitcher rings as it draws cold water from the well. Having washed away all traces of grease and mud, the flowers boast their fresh fragrance.
Amidst the whistling pines and wind, the tea cauldron boils; at the bright window, the recluse’s sleep is awakened. Chewing slowly on this sweet aroma, it gathers in the corners of the mouth;
its flavor is no different from the ferns of Mount Shouyang. In this clear poverty within the thatched cottage, the joy is boundless; how much more so when one searches for verses in song!
There is the moon upon the plum branches. At the Five Tombs, jade-like tears drench the rich delicacies; who would have known that the flavors of vegetables differ as vastly as heaven and abyss?
After the tea, the staff in hand awakens a pure inspiration; one turns once more from mountain behind to mountain before.
Congratulations on the Passing of Master Weng of Tiantong (Reborn at Eighty with a Single Tooth):
The old gourmand, reborn at eighty with a single tooth, Chews the void until it is well-masticated and spits out the dregs. He adorns the grasses beneath Linglong Rock;
Every branch and every leaf is a *tánhuā* (cloud-flower).
Sending off a monk to visit Master Chijue of Taibai and Master Shixi:
Before the plaque hung as Bao Gong, after the plaque hung as Bao Gong—manifesting in many bodies to preach the Dharma at Linglong. In seeking and visiting, there is no need to discuss host and guest;
the twelve gates of the face are fundamentally one and the same.
Sending off Attendant Wù: He went to visit Master Yǎnxī of Yùwáng;
amidst the deep, lush shade, he struck the cold ice. He washed his mother-born ears until they were clear. Blocking them, he would no longer listen for the call of "Xiǎoyù.
With the wind at his back, he came to hear the sound of Yǎnxī.
The Master Yunwo of the Jiedai Hermitage:
we look up to his legacy as a true transmission. His reception of people rests entirely upon the side of the mattock; when the occasion arises, he uses no idle lamentation.
There, the spring mountains naturally offer their wild herbs, raising their fists.
Congratulations to Master Bian of Mount Shan.

Having departed from the Twin Trees for Jinshan, he rises from his samādhi at the twin *tao* trees when the third watch of the night begins. He rides backward upon the golden tortoise, sporting across the eight directions;
the mallet in his sleeve strikes with a harsh, piercing sound, such that De-yun dares not take the lead.
Sending off Chan Master Jian from Tiantong to Jiangxin Donggu:

His lifelong existence has been one of utter poverty. I trouble you, my friend, to tell Elder Brother Liao: "Ever since he dwelt in the phoenix’s roost and the dragon’s nest, no one has entered the jeweled hall to walk beneath the bright moon."
The Head Seat Hetian Tongxin left the world, leaning on his staff;

having ceased weaving reed sandals, he retired to support his parents. Now entering the eye of a gnat, he stirs up clouds and dust, employing only the hand that delivers the Yunmen shout to further link with one person of Linglong.
In ancient times, before the Seven Buddhas, they were already being flaunted; clearly, they are but a single piece of rotten, withered firewood.
Old Lu did not know how to shoulder them; now there is no place to bury the embers.

Returning from a visit to Dai at the snowy shore, he moors his boat; frozen clouds lock the sky as jade-like flowers drift down. Having finished fishing in his reed cloak, he seeks out his companions;
unaware that white gulls are now flying near the bank.
The Hū monk with missing teeth and no learning is full of antics; he beats a drum in empty space and sings a folk song.
The mountains, rivers, and great earth laugh aloud together—what can be done about the deaf ears of such a man?
The Mirror Hall is neither bright nor dark, nor is it a stand; let myriad forms come forth as reflections at will.
Just as Old Lu broke through the wall with his writing—where there was no dust, yet there was dust.
The style of the western window was personally transmitted from the patriarch’s house; beneath the short eaves, the setting sun is often seen slanting.
Behold how he opened wide the eye that penetrates all directions—when the ox passes through, its tail still remains exposed.
How many times has the spring breeze played its melodies in the ancient peach immortal’s garden? After three thousand years, the fruit has finally matured.
Once, with a single drop of blood from a branch-tip, he exchanged it for the two eyes of Lingyun.
A stretch of cool shade at Songzhou has existed since time immemorial. Vaguely, Linji’s own hand planted it. Branch after branch, leaf after leaf, they hang with clear dew;
it causes the eyes of everyone in the entire city to open.
Stone-well striking hard, the effort reaches deep; who would have known there was dust beneath the water? Letting loose a single thread of the path brings life;
how many clear-eyed people has it deceived and led astray?

An ancient patchwork robe, half-draped over the shoulders, embraces a fragment of lingering cloud. Transmitted by the Seven Buddhas down to the present day, at this point where it is so tattered it cannot even be lifted,
the morning sun is just right for applying the golden needle.

The myriad phenomena, the ten thousand images, are all the seal of the enlightened mind; there is not a single thing that can be categorized as distant or intimate. Daming sat upon this and made it his nest;
until the end of his days, he never once knew how to turn himself around.
To Master Shixi: Returning from Yandang to Yanfeng, he carves jade to lock away the layered shadows;
it is as if the face of the Yangzhai miasma in Mei County has been touched by spring. Turning his head, he beats the poison drum that pierces the heavens;
how many more than thirteen people must have voices of such resentment?
Inscription on Old Rong’s *Picture of the Herd of Oxen*:
Three by three, five by five, they frolic across the level marshes; Treading upon the spring wind, the hundred grasses wither.
Do not paint the monk of Mount Mui— Lest people mistake it for a portrait of the Patriarch.

Inscription on a Sitting-Meditation Frog (with White Lotus Below) Once I have clearly realized my true nature, I am too weary to produce the drumming and blowing sounds of the spring pond. Leisurely, I lock fast the six sense-gates;
The fragrance of white lotuses wafts as the water and wind grow pure.
In a minor Buddhist service,

when the Japanese Master Gensha was preparing his coffin and had not yet stepped onto the deck of the boat, he had already traveled throughout the various patriarchs of the Great Tang, clearly knowing that what is realized is itself empty; yet he had not yet understood—
Born together and dying together. (Gesturing toward the reliquary shrine, he says: Here one sees the true intimacy; there is another path for turning back.
The blue-green seas and mountains are marked in countless layers.

This reveals the mind of the Superior Man’s entry into nirvana through fire, and the meaning of birth and death: whether manifest or hidden, there is no difference; the holy and the ordinary are of one essence. If you see this clearly, its application will be intimate and direct;
the fire shall burn away the thorns for three thousand li.
Guangxi Tang entered the bones [of realization] at Damei, yet could not remain there; before Xiaoduo Peak, he could not be pushed away. Now, both going and staying are without reliance;
directly beneath, one clarifies the "living word" within death. Piercing through the skull and sweeping away the mysterious path, the spiritual trace is no longer found.
At the place where the ape cries, Xitan Qikan’s death dwells within the mountain mind;
his life penetrates the universal eye. Having found the path, he travels freely, entirely without fetters—the profound barrier of the thousand sages.
A misstep and it is overturned; the five-colored auspicious qilin strides upon the celestial shore.

Zang Xianshou’s locked meditation cell attained the sublime essence of the Tiantai school; the shadow of the revolving pearl leaves no trace. Birth and death are but a fleeting play; concentration and wisdom are transcended, beyond dual cultivation.

What need is there here to speak of Zhuang Zhou dreaming he was a butterfly, or the butterfly dreaming it was Zhuang Zhou? All the sturdy locks are snapped shut; the clouds disperse, and the autumn fills the heavens.
This refreshing clarity is the very marrow of Master Dongshan.
Linji’s cool tree; Dongshan’s tile-drum song. Few rest in its shade; many listen for its resonance.
When the roots of death are severed, the sound of the tile drum fades away. Bones and melody have been exchanged; what prevents one from rolling into the thicket of complications?

Master Jiao bathes; bones rise from the emerald peaks as clouds disperse, and the moon shines bright upon the azure pool. Entirely free from dust—what is it that he bathes? If you act thus, you are a corpse on level ground;
if you do not act thus, you lose your reflection before the skull. Before the pivot of the mechanism there is a path straight as a bowstring. Jiao!
Does the master of the bath know? To step out the door is to encounter weeds.

Master Zhang’s iron thorn-bramble for locking his coffin is cast away from his face; he shatters the barrier between life and death, leaving no trace whatsoever—valued as little as a mere jade tablet.
Precious yet resembling dust; the whole lump split open into a chaotic mess. Not chaotic: interlocking rings, hooked and locked, cannot be extracted even with a blade.
Upādyāya Liang’s coffin-lock (a temporary arrival).
The void preaches the sutras; he is a man outside the gates of Vulture Peak. Directly beneath him, the thieving mind dies;
with eyes staring from within a coffin, a single pivot turns, and the stars and constellations shift. The mysterious barriers of Buddhas and Patriarchs are all locked and severed.
At Vulture Peak, the fire descends for the monkeys;
red trees nestle among the clouds. Ancient vines hang from the moon; with a single swift flight, they let out three clear chants.

Directly beneath, clinging and grasping cease; the path of the mind of birth and death is cut off. No longer shall they wander among the various species. (Hurling the torch, he says: What is this mass of fire?
Hindering the attendance of Shengre;
a record of the sayings of the Elder Master Xiu (concluded).
The Elder Master Fojian tempered his junior disciples with the "fire of both civil and military arts," during which many had their eyebrows singed away. [He] picked it up...
Those who have grasped the nostrils [of the Way] are but few; I hope only that my elder Dharma-brother will transcend the common herd.
As you first take charge of this famous monastery, upholding its essential principles, there is the "Path Above" (shangxiang yilu), slippery and perilous as a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.
Yet you do not realize that these two words, "perilous" and "slippery," are no less formidable than Yunmen’s Single-Word Barrier. As for the vital energy of life (shengji)...
The entire path is like grasping the edge of a frosty blade; who would dare look upon it with a direct eye? Moreover, this has already been certified by the masters.
My junior disciple Jujing has compiled these into a volume and requests that I provide a commentary for its conclusion. Although I am not clever, I cannot decline on principle.

Furthermore, how could I dare add gold to the yellow or slander that what has settled lacks fragrance? In the year Jǐmǎo (1059), while residing at Xuědòu, his younger brother Jūnjì wrote this colophon.
The bhikṣu Huìxiǎo of Japan, having come to study, made a donation for its publication.
Appendix:

Chan Master Baoyun Xiao, upon his return to the kingdom, made a donation to have one volume of the sayings of my late teacher, Venerable Hiseou, carved into woodblocks for me to send back at once; he did not have time to print many copies.
Residing at the Yun Tower of my late teacher’s former friend in Xijing,
I respectfully present this to the various Dharma brothers, the Zen masters of Tōfuku-ji.
This is Zen Master Byakun Kō of the Great Zen Temple Tōfuku-ji in the Kingdom of Japan, regarding the late teacher, Preceptor Kisei.
Within this assembly, I have seen through the very source of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Having gathered for a long time, many have come to know my heart.
I heard that on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the Dingyou year, he spoke a verse and entered nirvana. Being far away at the edge of the world, my grief and longing are beyond measure.
Having been graced by my brother’s visit, I have learned the full details; I therefore respectfully offer two verses of my own—one in lamentation and one sent forth—to express my feelings.
With sincere feelings, I humbly request your perusal at the site of the Weiyun Pagoda for Master Shouxi Zou.
This is respectfully presented by the junior disciple (Jujing) to the various venerable Zen masters of the Rib棘庵 (Lispik-an) in Japan:
A single sheet of white clouds returns to the sea eastward; may it universally bestow the rain of Dharma to transform fish and dragons.
Vairambha suddenly blows them all away, And across the great earth, their traces are hard to find.

The Buddha-dharma originally knows no division of self and other; Within this single world-system of Great Tang and Japan, The late master’s staff was as heavy as a mountain— How joyful to hear that there are now those who can bear it!
Written respectfully by Xia Jing in the middle summer of the third year of the Dàdé era (Jǐhài), the year 1059.
I previously sent a copy of the *Recorded Sayings* of my late teacher, along with a verse, for distribution and publication to the White Clouds.
Fearing it may not have reached you, Brother Meng, I have rewritten this and respectfully sent it to you once more.
